title: Shipment Pricing Refactor

title: Patient Vitals Monitor
flaw: useEffect fetching vitals on patientId change has no guard against out-of-order responses, so a stale fetch for a previously selected patient can resolve after a newer one and silently overwrite the currently displayed patient's vitals - an async race condition that only shows up when requests resolve out of order.
key_learnings: useEffect's cleanup runs right before the effect re-runs for a new dependency value (or on unmount) - it's the hook for marking a previous render's in-flight async work as stale.

AbortController only cancels anything if the signal is actually threaded into the request *and* every implementation (real fetch and test fakes) respects it - calling .abort() on a controller nobody passed the signal to is a no-op.
mistakes: First attempt had no cleanup/guard at all, so a stale response could freely overwrite newer state.
Second attempt added an AbortController but never passed abort.signal into fetchVitals, so .abort() had nothing to cancel - same bug persisted.
review_changes: Walked through a local didCancel flag set in the effect's cleanup and checked in .then()/.catch() before calling setState.

Walked through the full AbortController version: extending FetchVitals to accept a signal, threading it into the real fetch(), special-casing AbortError in .catch(), and updating test fakes to honor the signal.
next_focus: Another exercise in the same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect family before advancing categories, so it can be mastered before moving on.

title: Watchlist Quote Panel
flaw: useEffect fetching a quote on symbol change has no guard against out-of-order responses, so a stale fetch for a previously selected symbol can resolve after a newer one and silently overwrite the currently displayed symbol's quote - same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect race as the prior exercise, held at the same difficulty since that one's status was 'struggled'.
key_learnings: A didCancel-style flag scoped inside the effect's own closure (not a ref) is what flips false in that run's cleanup, so a stale .then()/.catch() belonging to the previous symbol can tell it's no longer current even without AbortController involved.

Threading the AbortController itself into FetchQuote's own signature (rather than constructing one outside and hoping the implementation respects it) is what made cancellation real this time, instead of repeating the prior exercise's abort.signal-never-passed-in mistake.

Keeping a possibly-unstable fetchQuote prop in a ref and leaving it out of the polling effect's dependency array avoids restarting the fetch/poll cycle on every inline-callback re-render, while still using its latest value on the next tick.
mistakes: No functional mistakes in the submitted fix - only a stylistic nit: the `quote.symbol !== symbol` checks in both the hook and the render fallback are redundant once the active-flag/abort guard is in place, since a mismatched quote can never reach state to begin with.
review_changes: Walked through why the prior exercise's AbortController attempt didn't work (signal constructed but never passed into fetchVitals) versus this one, which puts the AbortController in FetchQuote's own signature so any real implementation is forced to receive it.

Walked through the closure-scoped active flag as the mechanism that actually blocks the stale overwrite - cleanup flips it false right before the next effect run, so the earlier symbol's in-flight .then()/.catch() already knows it's stale before it ever checks the abort signal.

Reran the full suite against the original unmodified starter.tsx: both tests this submission added (the out-of-order stale-quote regression and the 2-second auto-refresh poll) fail on the bug and pass on the fix, confirming they actually exercise the race rather than passing vacuously.
next_focus: Category has landed 'completed' - clear to advance the rotation to architecture tradeoffs for the next newly-generated exercise.

Exercises 4-8 (Username Availability Field, Listing Detail Panel, Route Quote Panel, Semester Grades Panel, Fleet Health Panel) are still a pushed-but-unreviewed backlog in this same race-condition family - worth bringing those back for review too as extra reps now that the pattern has clicked.
Next time this pattern shows up, try the plain closure-flag fix directly in the component without reaching for a custom hook/ref abstraction, to keep the minimal version fluent too.

title: Username Availability Field
flaw: Debounced username-availability check has no guard against out-of-order async resolution: the effect keyed on the debounced value calls checkAvailability and sets status/suggestion directly in .then()/.catch() with no comparison against the current debounced value or a request id, so if an earlier keystroke's slower check resolves after a later keystroke's faster one, the stale result silently overwrites the status (and Continue-button enablement) for the username currently in the box - same stale-closure/out-of-order-async-effect race as the prior two exercises, held at the same difficulty and category since the last one (WatchlistQuotePanel) is still unreviewed/assigned and the category hasn't yet landed a 'completed' status since the original 'struggled' entry.

title: Ranked Queue Service
flaw: MatchmakingQueue exposes its internal `players` array as a public, directly-mutable field instead of encapsulating it, so the VIP 'boost to front' admin helper (and any future caller) can unshift players in without going through enqueue's maxSize and duplicate-membership checks - a broken-encapsulation/leaky-abstraction problem where the class can no longer guarantee its own invariants once any external code touches the array directly.
key_learnings: Correctly diagnosed the core fix: make `players` private and turn `boostToFront` into a method, so every mutation is forced through the class's own checks instead of being reachable from outside.

Split enqueue's size/duplicate checks into their own reusable methods so boostToFront (and future methods) could call into the same checks - good instinct for avoiding a second copy of the invariant logic.

For an already-queued player, chose splice-out-then-unshift over a swap-with-front-element specifically to preserve the relative order of every other player in the queue - correctly reasoned that a swap would disturb two players' positions instead of one, which matters for a matchmaking queue's fairness/ordering semantics.

Party Queue: checked capacity for the whole group before enqueueing any of them, so the group is added atomically and always ends up adjacent; added an optional partyId for future group-aware dequeue logic.
Discussed via chat rather than submitted as code for this session - approach was described and reasoned through verbally, not verified against the exercise's own test suite.
mistakes: Applied the same 'is there space' size check to both branches of boostToFront: the brand-new-player branch (where it's correct, since that's a net +1 on the queue) and the already-queued-player branch (where it's wrong, since splice-then-unshift is net +0 - moving someone already counted in the queue doesn't need any additional space). As written, boosting a player who's already in a full queue - the single most common time someone would actually want this - would be incorrectly rejected, even though it can never violate the max-size invariant.
review_changes: Walked through why gating both branches behind the same size check is a boundary-condition bug: the check only protects the case where the queue's total count actually grows, not the case where an existing member is just being repositioned.

Discussed splice+unshift vs. swap-with-front-element as two ways to move an existing player to the front, and confirmed splice+unshift is the better call for preserving the rest of the queue's relative order - swap would silently reorder a second, uninvolved player too.
next_focus: When a shared guard gets reused across multiple branches during a refactor, check whether the guard's condition is actually true for each branch individually (net change to the invariant it protects), rather than copying it because the mutation 'feels' similarly risky.

This session's review was conversational (no code pushed/tested) - worth doing a from-scratch coded pass on a similar encapsulation-smell exercise at some point to confirm the fix holds up against the actual test suite, not just verbal description.

title: Payroll Event Processor
flaw: PayrollEvent models four mutually-exclusive event shapes as one flat interface with a `type` discriminator plus a pile of unrelated optional fields, instead of a discriminated union - so an event object can carry fields that don't belong to its type (or omit required ones) with no compile error, and toLineItem's final branch is an unconditional catch-all ('correction - and, for now, anything else') with no exhaustiveness check, so a new event type added later silently falls into the correction branch (wrong description, wrong amount) instead of failing to compile. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. First appearance of the typescript-modeling category.

title: Product Grid Search
flaw: ProductGrid passes a brand-new inline arrow function as ProductCard's onAddToCart prop on every render, which defeats ProductCard's React.memo wrapper - so every visible card re-renders on each keystroke in the unrelated search input, even though each card's own product data hasn't changed; at full catalog scale this is a real rendering-performance cost on every character typed. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. First appearance of the react-state-performance category.

title: Lineup Eligibility Rules
flaw: canAddToLineup and canCompleteTrade independently re-implement the same player-eligibility rule rather than sharing one source of truth, and the two copies have already drifted: canAddToLineup blocks injured_reserve players from any slot except ir_slot, but canCompleteTrade never grew that check (its comment says IR players historically couldn't be traded at all), so a trade can currently place an injured_reserve player directly into a starter slot - a duplicated-business-rule-gone-stale smell rather than a crash. Regenerated to replace an earlier (incorrectly generated) debugging exercise - see exercise 5's note. title: Now Playing Crossfade
flaw: NowPlayingBar's track-change effect calls crossfade(...) but discards its returned cancel function instead of returning/storing it, so the interval crossfade starts is never cleared when the index changes again before that fade finishes - skipping again mid-fade leaves the previous interval running in the background, still calling setVolume against a track that's no longer current and overlapping with the new fade's calls. A missing-effect-cleanup/orphaned-interval bug, deliberately a different debugging sub-skill from exercises 2-4's async-fetch-ordering race family, now that that family landed 'completed' on exercise 3. Difficulty raised to 3 (third appearance of debugging, after struggled@2 then completed@2) and domain changed to avoid repeating the race-condition pattern yet again.
